tagline.text: A Palawan beach town where time moves slowly

children.text: A small beach town on the west coast between El Nido and Puerto Princesa, with barely a road or a pier, its relaxed pace is the draw. You can swim with sea turtles and island-hop deserted-island beaches much more quietly and cheaply than in El Nido.
Port Barton is a small fishing village in the municipality of San Vicente on Palawan's west coast. It's about
150km
north of Puerto Princesa and about
130km

south of El Nido, making it a popular midway stop for travelers moving between the two cities. The village lines a crescent-shaped bay with guesthouses and restaurants along the sandy beach, and dozens of islands and reefs are scattered in the waters offshore.

The village's biggest charm is its slowness. Bangkas beach directly onshore with no pier, and cars are almost nonexistent in the village, so you can walk the sandy paths barefoot. It used to be so remote that electricity from a generator ran only a few hours each evening, and even now that power supply has improved, frequent outages and slow internet naturally impose a kind of digital rest. This atmosphere has made it quietly beloved among European backpackers, who call it "El Nido ten years ago."

The sea here is every bit as beautiful as El Nido's. On an island-hopping trip you can cover, in a single day, a seagrass bed where sea turtles often appear, Twin Reef with its healthy coral, shallow water scattered with starfish, and deserted-island beaches like German Island and Exotic Island. It's rare for dozens of tour boats to crowd into one spot the way they do in El Nido, so you can enjoy it at a relaxed pace.

It suits travelers tired of the crowds at popular destinations, those who want to spend days lying in a hammock reading, and budget-conscious backpackers hoping to enjoy Palawan's sea affordably. It may be less convenient for travelers who need shopping, nightlife, or reliable internet.

A join tour departing from the village beach visits 3–5 islands and snorkeling spots. Routes are divided into Tours A, B, C, and so on, and lunch is often served at a deserted-island beach like German Island or Exotic Island.
In the shallow seagrass beds, you can get a close look at green sea turtles grazing. Keep at least
3m
from a turtle and never touch it.
Twin Reef, where coral splits into two branches, is a snorkeling spot rich in coral and tropical fish. In the shallow water off Starfish Island you can see starfish.
A forest waterfall about
4km
from the village, reached on foot in about
1 hour
or by motorbike. You can swim in the pool below, and the flow is fullest near the end of the rainy season.
A quiet beach over the headland north of the village, about
30–40 minutes
on foot or about
10 minutes
by bangka. A good place to spend half a day in the shade of the palms.
The village beach faces west, so you can watch the sun set over the sea every evening. Finishing the day with a cocktail in a hammock at a beach restaurant is daily life in Port Barton.
Rent one on the beach and paddle out across the calm bay toward a nearby island or the mangroves.

The nearest major airport is Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS), about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Manila, at around

one way. San Vicente also has a small airport, but scheduled flights are irregular, so most travelers use Puerto Princesa. You can also fly into El Nido Airport (ENI) and travel down after finishing your El Nido trip.
A shared van from Puerto Princesa airport or the San Jose terminal in the city to Port Barton takes about
3–4 hours
for around

. You can book a hotel pickup; the route runs along the Roxas-direction highway before turning onto the western mountain road near Salvacion, and this stretch is now fully paved, making the trip much smoother than before. Taking a Roxas-bound bus and switching to a jeepney or motorbike at the Salvacion junction is cheaper but takes longer. From El Nido it's about
4–5 hours
by shared van, around
A boat trip hopping between islands along the coast sometimes operates between El Nido and Port Barton. Whether it's running depends on the weather and the operator, so check locally.
You can walk everywhere within the village. For the waterfall or Long Beach direction, rent a motorbike (about
per day) or negotiate with a tricycle or motorbike driver.
November
through
May
is the dry season and good for visiting.
March
through
May
especially has the calmest sea and clearest water, the best time for island hopping and snorkeling. From
December
to
February
there are some windy days, but the cool temperatures make it good for trekking.
Port Barton is on the west coast, so it takes the full effect of the southwest monsoon Habagat from
June
to
October

. In this period, high waves often cancel island hopping or limit it to nearby islands only, and rain slows travel on the mountain road too. On the plus side, lodging is cheaper and the village gets even quieter. If you visit during the rainy season, it's best to schedule island hopping with some flexibility.

Lodging centers on guesthouses and bungalows lining the village beach. A backpacker dorm runs about
per night, a fan bungalow about
, and an air-conditioned beach bungalow or small resort about

. A spot right on the beach gets the best sunset views but can have restaurant noise in the evening, while the village interior is quieter and cheaper. For somewhere even more secluded, you can choose a resort on a nearby island reached by bangka, or around White Beach. Rooms fill up fast in peak season, so book ahead.

The food centers on fresh seafood barbecue at beach restaurants. In the evening, beach restaurants grill the day's catch of fish, squid, and shrimp over charcoal, and many also serve dishes like coconut curry and seafood pasta suited to Western travelers' tastes. Small Filipino restaurants in the village serve home-style dishes like adobo, sinigang, and pancit for about
per person. A few European-run bakeries and cafes are good for breakfast too. Island-hopping lunches typically feature grilled fish, pork, rice, and fruit served on a deserted-island beach.
The village has no ATM, or one that's often out of order, and cards are almost never accepted. Bring enough cash from Puerto Princesa or El Nido to cover your whole stay.
Power has improved but outages are still frequent, so it's a good idea to bring a power bank and a flashlight.
The internet is slow and unstable, so if you have work or urgent calls to make, bring SIM cards from both Smart and Globe, and handle anything important before you arrive.
You can book island hopping at a tour booth on the beach or through your accommodation on your first day, for departure the next day. It's worth comparing routes and inclusions across a few booths.
Bangkas beach directly on the sand, so you'll wade in up to your knees when boarding or disembarking. Pack your belongings in a dry bag.
At night, the beach and lanes have little lighting, so a flashlight comes in handy.
Local guides say your odds of meeting a sea turtle are best in the morning.
Touching, chasing, or riding a sea turtle is prohibited and can carry a penalty if caught. Follow your guide's instructions and keep your distance while observing.
Wear a life vest on the bangka, and don't insist on going out on high-wave days.
The beach sand has many sand flies, and a bite can itch severely for days, so bring insect repellent.
The nearest large hospital is in Puerto Princesa, several hours away. Bring basic medicine and travel insurance.
Environmental fee and tour rules can change by decision of the San Vicente tourism office, so check the latest notices.
In the rainy season, landslides or washed-out roads can occur on the mountain road, so check road conditions before traveling.
